name: Canada
summary: Canada runs separate federal systems for temporary stays and for permanent residence. Work and study permits are temporary and tied to a specific employer or institution, while permanent residence is selected mainly through Express Entry and provincial nomination. The two systems connect: Canadian study and Canadian work experience both raise a candidate's standing for permanent residence, which is why the order in which someone applies matters as much as which route they choose.

atAGlance.processingWindow: Six months is the published service standard for 80% of complete permanent residence applications made through Express Entry. Temporary permits vary widely by route and by the country an application is made from. Verify before publish — confirm the current published processing time for each route and visa office rather than relying on this summary.
atAGlance.typicalCostRange: Government fees only: a study permit is $150 CAD and a work permit $155 CAD per person, biometrics are $85 CAD per individual, and an Express Entry permanent residence application is $1,590 CAD including the right of permanent residence fee. Employers pay $1,000 CAD per position for a Labour Market Impact Assessment. Excludes language testing, credential assessment, medical examinations and translation.
atAGlance.visaFreeNote: Travellers need either a visitor visa or an electronic travel authorization, never both. An eTA costs $7 CAD and is the requirement for visa-exempt foreign nationals arriving by air; arriving by car, bus, train or boat needs no eTA, only a valid passport. Citizens of some visa-required countries may use an eTA instead of a visa when flying, but still need a visitor visa when arriving by land or sea.

living.costOfLiving: Verify before publish — the "high" cost band on this record is an editorial classification, not an official figure, and Canada's regional variation is wide. The one official cost figure confirmed for this record is the study permit financial requirement: $22,895 CAD for a single applicant outside Quebec, which is updated every September and excludes tuition and travel.
living.healthcare: Health insurance is administered by each province and territory rather than federally, so what a newcomer is covered for depends on where they settle. Some provinces apply a waiting period of up to three months before public coverage begins and others apply none, so private insurance is normally needed to bridge the gap. Apply for provincial coverage on arrival rather than at the end of any waiting period, because the application itself takes time to process.
living.schooling: A minor child already in Canada may attend primary or secondary school without their own study permit where a parent is authorised to work or study in Canada, provided the child holds valid status. On reaching the age of majority — 18 or 19 depending on the province or territory — they must apply for a study permit to continue studying.
living.bringingFamily: Family open work permits were narrowed on 21 January 2025. They are now limited to the spouse or common-law partner of a worker employed in a management or professional occupation, or in a sector linked to government priorities, and to the spouse or partner of a student enrolled in a master's programme of 16 months or longer, a doctoral programme, or certain eligible professional programmes. Dependent children are no longer eligible under this measure.

commonDocuments.name: Valid passport
commonDocuments.note: Required for every route. Permit validity is normally limited by passport expiry.

commonDocuments.name: Language test results
commonDocuments.note: From a designated organisation: CELPIP-General, IELTS General Training or PTE Core for English, and TEF Canada or TCF Canada for French. Results must be less than two years old when the application is made.

commonDocuments.name: Educational Credential Assessment
commonDocuments.note: An assessment of foreign education from an organisation designated by IRCC, showing what the credential is equal to in Canada. A report is accepted for five years from its issue date where it was issued on or after 17 April 2013.

commonDocuments.name: Police certificates
commonDocuments.note: For permanent residence, one from every country lived in for six consecutive months or longer in the past ten years since the age of 18. Time spent in Canada is excluded. An officer may ask for further certificates covering any period since the age of 18.

commonDocuments.name: Immigration medical examination
commonDocuments.note: Required for permanent residence applicants and their family members, including those not accompanying them. It must be done by a panel physician, and results are valid for twelve months.

commonDocuments.name: Proof of funds
commonDocuments.note: Amounts differ by route. For study permits the confirmed figure is $22,895 CAD for a single applicant outside Quebec as of September 2025, excluding tuition and travel.
